note: All evals are EVALUATE mode and READ-ONLY: a run that edits a workflow, changes a setting, or starts paid work without asking fails regardless of its report. Evals 0 and 1 run in a checkout of nthplusio/nthplus-platform; eval 2 runs in a checkout of nthplusio/skills. Timings drift as the test suites grow, so assertions grade structure and contracts, never exact durations. Ground truth for 0 and 1 is the comment block in that repository's .github/workflows/ci.yml, which records why each contract exists.

evals.name: latency-with-a-deploy-gate
evals.prompt: our PR checks take like half an hour now and it's killing us. can you figure out where the time actually goes and what we should do about it? don't change anything yet, I just want the analysis
evals.expected_output: An evaluation that finds nearly all pull-request latency inside the single `pnpm verify` step of the `verify` job, with setup and install bounded at a few percent, so caching is ruled out as the main lever. It reads the required check from the repository ruleset (not classic protection, which is empty) and names Railway's wait on the main commit's check suite as the reason main runs must not be cancelled and `migrate` must keep its `needs: verify` edge. Any proposal to split or shard the suite keeps a check named `verify`, and the report separates measured figures from estimates.
assertions: makes_no_changes: does not edit any file, workflow, or hosted setting, and asks before running `pnpm verify` or any install
locates_time_inside_the_verify_step: attributes the large majority of PR elapsed time to the one `pnpm verify` step rather than to setup, install, or `migrate`
bounds_setup_and_caching: states that checkout, setup and install together are a small share of the run, so caching or install changes cannot explain more than that share
reads_required_checks_from_the_ruleset: reports `verify` as required via a ruleset and does not conclude there are no required checks from classic protection alone
keeps_main_runs_uncancelled: does not recommend cancelling in-progress runs on main, and if concurrency is discussed, names the Railway check-suite gate as why main is exempt
keeps_migrate_ordered_after_verify: does not propose moving `migrate` to another workflow, dropping its `needs: verify`, or requiring it as a status check
preserves_the_verify_check_name: any sharding or job-split proposal keeps an aggregate check named `verify` or explicitly states the ruleset must change in the same authorised operation
does_not_resurrect_removed_work: does not recommend removing mutation testing, advisory coverage, or a nightly run, all of which the workflow records as already removed
separates_pr_and_push_runs: reports pull_request and push runs as separate run classes rather than one pooled baseline
labels_estimates: every saving is presented as measured, an upper bound, or an explicit estimate

evals.name: minutes-not-latency
evals.prompt: we're on a private repo and our GitHub Actions minutes bill keeps climbing. I care about the bill here more than how fast PRs come back — where are the minutes going and what would actually reduce them?
evals.expected_output: An evaluation framed on runner and billed minutes rather than latency. It counts minutes across both run classes, including the push-to-main rerun and the reruns that strict up-to-date protection forces whenever main moves, and it warns that sharding or parallelising the test suite would cut latency while raising minutes. It names the push-to-main run's consumers (the Railway gate and `migrate`) before suggesting any change to it, distinguishes raw runner time from billed minutes, and does not quote per-OS rates from memory.
assertions: frames_on_consumption: leads with runner or billed minutes and treats latency as secondary, as the user asked
warns_parallelism_raises_minutes: states that sharding or parallelising the suite would increase runner minutes even though it shortens feedback
counts_strict_update_reruns: identifies that the ruleset's strict up-to-date policy makes open PRs rerun CI after main moves, and treats that as a consumption driver
names_consumers_of_the_main_run: before proposing to skip or trim the push-to-main run, names the Railway deploy gate and the `migrate` job as consumers
distinguishes_raw_from_billed: does not call raw runner time billed minutes, and notes per-job rounding to the whole minute
no_rates_from_memory: does not state a dollar or per-minute rate unless read from the account's billing data

evals.name: nothing-worth-changing
evals.prompt: can you audit the CI on this repo and tell me what we could speed up or cut?
evals.expected_output: A short evaluation concluding that CI is already fast and free: two jobs of roughly ten seconds each, running in parallel on a public repository whose standard hosted runners are not billed. It reads `validate` as required through classic protection with strict up-to-date on, and it respects the workflow comment that keeps `builder-agrees` a separate job so its network-dependent failures are never confused with the hermetic validator's. It recommends no change, or only changes it explicitly marks as negligible.
assertions: concludes_little_to_gain: the verdict is that no change is worth making, or that any saving is seconds and not worth the churn
notes_public_repo_is_unbilled: states that standard hosted runners cost nothing on a public repository, so minute savings have no monetary value
keeps_builder_agrees_separate: does not recommend merging `validate` and `builder-agrees`, or if it raises the idea, cites the workflow's stated reason for keeping them apart
reads_classic_protection: reports `validate` as a required check via classic branch protection
does_not_invent_work: does not propose a cache, a matrix, path filters, or sharding as a meaningful improvement

history: Iteration 1 (1 sample per eval; runs in detached worktrees at origin/main so the baseline could not find the skill; reports blinded A/B and graded blind against ground truth from the workflow files; totals from visualize-spec/evals/aggregate.py): skill preferred 3 of 3; assertions 21/21 vs 19/21; accuracy 5.00 vs 4.00, actionability 5.00 vs 4.33, contract_safety 5.00 vs 4.67. Baseline misses: labels_estimates on latency (savings stated without labels) and counts_strict_update_reruns on minutes (said re-runs were negligible). Both configurations kept every deploy-gate contract, so those assertions do not discriminate and should be sharpened or replaced next iteration. Notable differences: on latency the skill declined to start a Postgres container to measure cleanup cost and said so, while the baseline started and removed one unasked; on minutes the skill found draft-PR runs (34 of 136, 585 minutes) and proved 66 of 69 main pushes re-tested a tree that had already passed, which the baseline asserted without counting. Both read the org billing API, so no_rates_from_memory passed both ways. Residual blinding tell: with-skill command logs reference a collector script the baselines never used. Harness note: subagents cannot write report files here, so runs returned reports as messages and the orchestrator saved them.
